contributions.headingText: Early T-precursor lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma (ETP-ALL) is a neoplasm composed of blasts committed to the T-cell lineage with a unique immunophenotype that includes the expression of stem cell markers and/or myeloid lineage markers.
2A71 & XH8F29 Precursor T-lymphoblastic neoplasms & Early T-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukaemia

Patients typically present with bone marrow and peripheral blood involvement. Some patients may present with lymphoblastic lymphoma {34297047; 26747249; 22994934}. Lymph node and hepatosplenic involvement is common. Mediastinal involvement is detected in 10–40% of patients {26747249; 22829239; 32974153; 31537688}. CNS involvement is reported in as many as 18% of patients {26747249; 22829239; 31537688}.

Symptoms and signs at presentation are related to cytopenias or manifestations of extramedullary disease. The white blood cell count may or may not be elevated, and in some studies, patients with ETP-ALL tend to have a lower white blood cell count than those with non-ETP ALL {33026184}.

ETP-ALL represents 12–17% of paediatric T-lymphoblastic leukaemia (T-ALL) cases {26853647; 19147408; 29519867} and 22–40% of adult cases {28605290; 22829239; 31115909}. In the adult population, patients with ETP-ALL tend to be older than those with non-ETP ALL {31115909; 22829239; 32368831}.

The etiology is unknown in most cases. Genome-wide association studies previously demonstrated several susceptibility loci for T-ALL. In a recent study, germline RUNX1 variants were enriched in ETP-ALL; and in a mouse model, RUNX1 variants cooperated with mutated JAK3 to induce ETP-ALL {34166225}.

ETP-ALL was initially recognized as a distinct type of T-ALL on the basis of a gene expression signature that overlaps with that of normal early T-precursors {19147408}. Physiologically, these precursors are the earliest recognizable stage in T-cell ontogeny and represent recent immigrants from the bone marrow to the thymus. They are characterized by multilineage differentiation potential and the expression of lymphoid, myeloid, and stem cell markers {18401411; 18401412}. In an analogous manner, ETP-ALL is characterized by a specific transcriptional signature close to that of haematopoietic stem cells and myeloid progenitors {22237106}. Single-cell RNA sequencing also showed that leukaemic cells express plasticity, with both stem cell and T-cell signatures, and can differentiate to stimulate an immunosuppressive microenvironment through the expression of the checkpoint molecule LGALS9 and the support of dysfunctional CD8+ T cells {33227818}. The expression profile of ETP-ALL is characterized by increased expression of MEF2C {21481790} and decreased expression of BCL11B {33876209; 34402058} and GATA3 {19934022; 23359050}.

A recent murine molecular pathogenesis model postulates concurrent EZH2 and RUNX1 inactivating mutations as initiating events leading to the expansion of early thymic progenitors with an ETP-ALL gene expression signature whose leukaemic potential is further promoted by the acquisition of mutations (e.g. FLT3), resulting in the constitutive activation of the RAS signalling pathway {29438697}. This model recapitulates the distinctive mutation profile of ETP-ALL, which resembles that of myeloid neoplasms and is characterized by activating mutations in genes regulating cytokine receptor and RAS signalling (FLT3, NRAS, KRAS, IL7R, JAK3, JAK1, SH2B3, BRAF), haematopoietic development (GATA3, ETV6, RUNX1, IKZF1), and histone modifications (EZH2, EED, SUZ12, SETD2, EP300) {22237106; 23603912; 23359050}. NOTCH1 mutations are uncommon in ETP-ALL, in contrast to other types of T-ALL {23359050}.

The frequency of CDKN2A/CDKN2B deletion is low in patients with ETP-ALL {31537688; 33306218; 34297047}.

The majority of ETP-ALL cases do not have TRG gene rearrangements, and they frequently lack biallelic deletion of the TRG locus, in contrast to non-ETP ALL, supporting an early maturation stage {23359050; 23975177; 31537688}.

In smears, lymphoblasts are small to medium in size and have round to convoluted nuclei, finely dispersed chromatin, small or absent nucleoli, and mildly to moderately basophilic cytoplasm {19147408}.

Histological sections show sheets of lymphoblasts with high N:C ratios, finely stippled chromatin, and inconspicuous nucleoli.

Immunophenotype

The ETP-ALL immunophenotype is defined as follows: (1) expression of cCD3, (2) absent CD1a and CD8 expression (< 5% positive blasts); (3) absent or dim CD5 expression (< 75% positive blasts); and (4) expression of one or more myeloid (CD11b, CD13, CD33, CD65, KIT [CD117]) and/or stem cell (CD34, HLA-DR) markers (≥ 25% positive blasts) {19147408; 26747249} (see #30747Box 5.04). The expression of CD123 has also been reported {30361418}. The ETP-ALL immunophenotype may be established by immunohistochemistry.

A proportion of ETP-ALL cases show heterogeneous expression of cCD3, with a subset of blasts being negative {32812702}. sCD3 is usually absent {31115909; 19147408}. CD7 is consistently positive, a feature that, when combined with the expression of stem cell or myeloid markers, provides a distinct phenotype for measurable residual disease evaluation by flow cytometry.

It has been suggested that defining ETP-ALL by immunophenotyping may lead to an underestimation of the number of cases of true ETP-ALL, relative to gene expression profiling {23975177; 20644084}. This may be due in part to the challenges of using a percentage threshold for CD5 expression. Proposed alternative approaches include using the absence of expression of CD4 instead of CD5, which in some studies allowed for a closer correlation between immunophenotype-based and gene expression profile–based designations {23975177; 31537688}. Other approaches incorporating scoring systems have also been proposed {31115909; 22128890}. T-ALL cases with an immunophenotype similar to that of ETP-ALL but with CD5 expression (in ≥ 75% of blasts) have been designated as near–ETP-ALL, but at present the clinical implications of such a designation remain unclear {33639000; 26747249}.

An initial diagnosis of ETP-ALL should not be based on flow cytometry on a peripheral blood sample, because of the potential immunophenotypic overlap with T/myeloid mixed-phenotype acute leukaemia (MPAL) and occasional immunophenotypic discordance between the circulating and medullary components of some acute leukaemia types {30255571}.

Differential diagnosis

Exclusion of MPAL as defined in this volume of the WHO classification requires particular attention, given the close biological relationship of ETP-ALL to T/myeloid MPAL. The initial definition of ETP-ALL incorporated a conservative threshold of < 3% to define negative myeloperoxidase expression by cytochemistry and flow cytometry {19147408}. This threshold may not be optimal for defining myeloperoxidase positivity for MPAL diagnosis, and further studies are needed to define the boundary between these neoplasms. Until further data are available, the original threshold of < 3% to define negative myeloperoxidase in ETP-ALL is retained.

Essential: lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma features by morphology; blasts must express an early T-precursor immunophenotype, characterized by the following (see #30747Box 5.04): positive for cCD3, absent CD1a and CD8 expression (< 5% positive blasts), absent or dim CD5 expression (< 75% positive blasts), expression of one or more myeloid (CD11b, CD13, CD33, CD65, KIT [CD117]) and/or stem cell (CD34, HLA-DR) markers (≥ 25% positive blasts), and negative myeloperoxidase (< 3%).

Clinical outcomes for children with ETP-ALL were initially reported to be poor when compared with non-ETP ALL, and similar outcomes were observed in adults {19147408; 22128890; 23065427; 26747249; 31537688; 33026184}. In subsequent years, several studies showed that long-term outcomes of paediatric and adult patients with ETP-ALL were comparable to those of patients with other T-ALLs {24708207; 26853647; 26123477; 28605290; 30028023; 34250504; 32813610}. Such favourable outcomes were reported despite higher rates of measurable residual disease after induction among patients with ETP-ALL. This could be due to treatment intensification for ETP-ALL patients with measurable residual disease and the increased rate of allogeneic stem cell transplantation after the first remission.

Because BCL2 is overexpressed in ETP-ALL, ongoing clinical trials are exploring BCL2 inhibition as a potential targeted therapy {24994123; 33593877}.
